problem: VLN agents are treated as black boxes: performance gaps to humans remain large (R2R 78 vs 86, RxR 53 vs 94, Touchdown 17 vs 92), yet little is known about how agents use instruction tokens, visual objects, and directions, or whether their vision-language alignment is reliable.
motivation: New architectures and training tricks bring only small gains, so locating what current agents actually understand can guide better model and task design. The paper applies counterfactual input interventions (masking or replacing tokens, masking objects, flipping views) at evaluation time, with controlled trials, to measure treatment effects on success.
key_idea: Diagnose nine pretrained VLN agents on R2R, RxR-en and Touchdown by ablating object, direction and numeric tokens in instructions and objects and directions in the visual environment at test time, with controlled random-masking baselines.
insight: Masking object or direction tokens hurts more than masking the same number of random tokens for indoor agents, but on Touchdown masking objects hurts less than random masking. Outdoor agents therefore mostly ignore objects, and direction masking causes drops up to -90% (ARC). Replacing tokens hurts Transformer agents more than masking them, which suggests better alignment and counting. Dynamically masking the visual objects mentioned in the instruction barely hurts (R2R SR stays above 44%), far less than masking the object tokens, so text dominates vision and the alignment is doubtful.
method: Instruction token ablation: uses the Stanza POS tagger (NOUN/PROPN) to find object tokens and a fixed word list (left, right, back, front, forward, stop) for direction tokens; masks them with [MASK] or replaces them with random tokens of the same type.
Controlled trial: randomly masks the same number of arbitrary tokens (or visual objects) to separate the effect of the token type from the effect of losing tokens; results are averaged over 5 runs.
Numeric token ablation: on the subset of instructions containing cardinals 1-20 or ordinals 1st-20th, masks or replaces numbers to test counting ability.

Visual object masking: uses Matterport object bounding boxes filled with the surrounding mean color; settings are mask all visible objects, mask foreground objects (within 3 m), and k random objects; a same-model EnvDrop check with ResNet-152 vs CLIP-ViT features confirms the trend.
Direction flip: horizontally flips viewpoint images so left and right are swapped, testing whether agents follow directions visually.
Alignment perturbation: replaces object tokens on the text side, and on the vision side dynamically masks the visual objects mentioned in the instruction, compared with masking the tokens.

setting.backbone: Nine existing pretrained agents used as-is: EnvDrop, FAST, VLN-BERT (Recur), PREVALENT, CLIP-ViL, VLN-HAMT, RCONCAT, ARC, VLN-Transformer
setting.training_data: No new training; author-released checkpoints trained on the original R2R / RxR-en / Touchdown training sets (plus each model's own augmentation or pre-training); ablations are applied only at evaluation.
setting.observation: Panoramic RGB (ResNet-152 or CLIP-ViT features indoor; ResNet-18 street-view features outdoor) plus text instructions
setting.action_space: Discrete navigation-graph viewpoints (indoor R2R/RxR) and Touchdown street-view graph nodes (outdoor)
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (R2R, RxR); Touchdown Street View environment
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object bounding-box annotations are used to build the visual ablations (analysis only)

numbers.extra: Released checkpoint; diagnostic study, not a proposed method

numbers_note: Diagnostic paper; the numbers are vanilla scores of existing agents, and most results are relative changes (%) under ablation. Other vanilla scores: VLN-BERT 53.3 and CLIP-ViL 40.21 SR; RCONCAT 11.78 and ARC 15.19 TC. Touchdown is not in the canonical benchmark list.
results: Indoor agents rely on both object and direction tokens (masking objects gives -20% to -48% SR) and consider background objects. Outdoor agents rely mainly on direction tokens (ARC -90%) and largely ignore objects. Transformer agents show better numeric reasoning and object alignment, but the small effect of masking visual objects relative to masking text tokens shows unbalanced use of vision and text.
limitations: Ablations are performed only at test time on pretrained agents, so out-of-distribution inputs may confound the effects.
Object and direction tokens are found by POS tagging and a small word list, and the study is correlational and does not propose a better agent.
Visual object ablation is only possible indoors, because Touchdown has no object annotations.
